pillar: China HIFU Leadership: The HAIFU Programme and Clinical Evidence

items.q: What is HIFU, and how does it treat a tumour without surgery?
items.a: HIFU uses focused ultrasound waves to heat and destroy a tumour from outside the body, with no cuts and no needles. Hundreds of beams pass harmlessly through skin and tissue, then converge on one point inside the tumour and raise it above 60°C within seconds. Real-time ultrasound or MRI guides each pulse. The dead tissue is slowly reabsorbed by the body over the following months.

items.q: Why is China considered the world leader in HIFU?
items.a: China built and approved the first clinical HIFU system, and the Chongqing HAIFU programme has treated more patients than any other centre worldwide. Chinese regulators cleared the technology in 1999, years ahead of most countries, which gave those teams two decades of case volume. That experience shows in published series covering uterine fibroids, liver, bone and pancreatic tumours. Access and suitability still depend on your diagnosis and your treating team.

items.q: Which cancers does the HAIFU programme actually treat?
items.a: The strongest published experience is in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer, bone sarcoma, kidney tumours and soft tissue tumours, alongside benign uterine fibroids. HIFU is often used when a tumour is inoperable, when surgery would carry too much risk, or to shrink a painful mass. In many cases it is combined with chemotherapy or radiotherapy rather than replacing them. Whether it suits your tumour type and location depends on imaging and specialist review.

items.q: How good is the evidence that HIFU works?
items.a: Evidence is strongest for pain relief and local tumour control, and weaker for overall survival. Trials in advanced pancreatic cancer report meaningful pain reduction in most patients, and Chinese bone sarcoma series report long-term limb preservation. Much of this data comes from single centres rather than large randomised trials, so results may not transfer to every patient. Your oncologist can weigh this evidence against standard options for your stage.

items.q: Does HIFU hurt, and will I be asleep for it?
items.a: Most patients are sedated or given light general anaesthesia, so the treatment itself is not painful. You lie still on a treatment table, often partly submerged in degassed water, for one to four hours depending on tumour size. Some people feel warmth, a dull ache or skin tenderness afterwards. Because nothing is cut, there is no wound to heal and hospital stays are usually short.

items.q: How long is recovery, and when can I fly home?
items.a: Most patients are up and walking the same day, and many leave hospital within one to three days. Teams often ask you to stay in the city for one to two weeks so imaging can confirm how much tumour was ablated before you travel. Skin redness, mild fever or fatigue can last several days. Fitness to fly is a judgement for the treating doctor, not a fixed rule.

items.q: What are the risks and side effects of HIFU?
items.a: The most common problems are skin burns, temporary nerve irritation and pain over the treated area, and these usually settle within weeks. Less often, nearby structures such as bowel, nerves or blood vessels can be injured, which is why tumour location matters so much. Fever and tiredness while dead tissue is reabsorbed are normal. Risk depends heavily on the tumour site and the experience of the centre.

items.q: How much does HIFU treatment in China cost?
items.a: A single HIFU session in a Chinese centre commonly falls between USD 6,000 and USD 15,000, before scans, hospital stay, interpreting and accommodation. Costs rise when several sessions are needed or when HIFU is combined with chemotherapy. Quotes vary widely between hospitals and change with tumour size and location. Ask for a written breakdown before you travel, as published prices are estimates and may not reflect your final bill.

items.q: Can I still have HIFU if my cancer has already spread?
items.a: Often yes, because HIFU is frequently used in advanced disease to control a painful or bulky tumour rather than to cure it. Doctors may treat one liver lesion or one bone deposit while systemic treatment continues. Eligibility depends on whether the tumour can be reached safely by the ultrasound beam and on your general fitness. Only a specialist reviewing your recent scans can confirm whether you qualify.

items.q: How do I arrange an assessment at a HIFU centre in China?
items.a: Start by sending recent scans, pathology reports and a treatment summary for remote review, since most centres decide suitability from imaging before anything is booked. Services such as CancerFax can help forward records to Chinese HIFU units and organise visas and travel. Any recommendation that comes back should be discussed with your own oncologist, who knows your full history and can advise whether travelling makes sense for you.
